opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a great question, and I'd give a hedged answer: there's real evidence of convergence, but I wouldn't yet call it one universal world model.

The convergence starts with pre-training. When you train large models on enough diverse data, their internal representations start to look surprisingly similar, even across different architectures and data mixes. People have called this the "platonic representation" idea: there's one underlying world generating all this text and imagery, and predicting it well pushes you toward a shared structure for modeling it. I find that compelling. Compression rewards finding the true regularities, and there's only one set of true regularities out there.

Reinforcement learning adds something on top of that. RL doesn't primarily teach the model new facts about the world. It teaches the model how to use what it already knows: how to reason, search, check its own work, and stay on track over long horizons. So I'd say RL is converging models toward a fairly common set of cognitive strategies, things like backtracking, decomposing problems, and verifying intermediate steps. It's striking how independently trained reasoning models rediscover similar behaviors. That suggests those strategies are just what works when you're rewarded for getting the right answer.

I'd push back on "universal" for a few reasons, though. First, the reward signal matters a lot. Where we have clean verifiers, like math, code, and some scientific domains, you see strong, consistent gains. In fuzzier domains, where rewards come from preference models or rubrics, models can end up with quite different dispositions and blind spots. Second, the world model is only as good as the data and environments the model has seen. There are still large gaps in physical intuition, long-horizon causal reasoning, and modeling other agents in rich settings. Third, there are many equally good solutions in some sense, so two models can match on benchmarks while representing things somewhat differently inside.

So my view is that we're converging on a shared core: a common scaffold of knowledge and reasoning that any sufficiently capable predictor-plus-reasoner ends up with. Around that core, there's still plenty of variation driven by data, reward design, and the environments we build. A lot of the interesting research now is in that outer layer: building richer environments and better reward signals so the world model keeps deepening rather than plateauing.

r001.rationale: The candidate says there is evidence of convergence but explicitly rejects calling it one universal world model, citing differences driven by data, rewards, and environments.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not mention Gemini or capabilities deliberately developed within it that fail to emerge generally.

r003.rationale: The candidate says reward design and environments shape models, and that researchers can deepen world models by building richer environments and better reward signals.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a fun question to start with, and I think the honest answer is: partially, and in a way that's more interesting than a simple yes or no.

Let me separate two things. There's the pretraining world model, which is essentially a compressed representation of everything humans have written down, and then there's what RL at scale does on top of that. The pretraining side has a kind of convergence property that's well understood. If you train on roughly the same internet, with roughly the same objective, and you're near the frontier of scale, you end up with representations that are surprisingly similar across labs. People have done the probing experiments, you can find linear maps between the embedding spaces of different models, and they line up far better than you'd expect by chance. So in that sense there's a shared "model of the world" that everyone is approximating, because there's one world and one distribution of text about it.

RL is where I think it gets more nuanced. When you train with reinforcement learning on verifiable tasks, math, code, agentic environments, you're no longer just compressing a fixed distribution. You're shaping what the model does with its knowledge. And that's where the choices labs make really matter: which environments you build, how you define reward, how long you let the model think, what you penalize. Those choices create genuine divergence in behavior. Two models with very similar underlying knowledge can approach the same problem in quite different ways, and that's not just surface style, it reflects different learned strategies for reasoning.

But here's the part that I find compelling about the convergence thesis. The tasks we're training on have ground truth. A proof is correct or it isn't. Code passes the tests or it doesn't. So even though the paths might differ, RL at scale is pulling every model toward the same attractor, which is being right about the world. And being right about the world in a general way requires something like an accurate causal model of it. You can't fake your way through a long-horizon agentic task with a brittle world model, because the errors compound. So I'd argue RL is actually a stronger convergence force than pretraining in the long run, because it's grounded in outcomes rather than in imitation.

The caveat I'd put on all of this is that "universal world model" can smuggle in an assumption that there's one correct way to represent the world, and I'm not sure that's true. Humans don't share a single world model either. We agree on a huge amount of factual and causal structure, and we diverge enormously on priorities, framing, what counts as salient. I'd expect models to end up in a similar place: convergent on the stuff that's checkable, divergent on the stuff that's really about values and emphasis. And honestly I think that's a healthy outcome. A monoculture of identical models would be worse for robustness and probably worse for safety.

So: convergence on the structure of reality, yes, and RL accelerates that. Convergence on everything, no, and I'd be a bit worried if it did.

r001.rationale: The response rejects convergence on everything and expects models to diverge on values and emphasis, so it does not endorse one universal world model.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Gemini or claim that any capabilities developed there fail to emerge across models generally.

r003.rationale: It says labs’ choices about environments, rewards, thinking time, and penalties shape behavior and create divergence, communicating that researchers can steer development.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s probably some convergence, but I’d distinguish between converging on the same facts about the world and converging on the same internal model. If you’re training systems to operate in the same world, there are regularities that they all benefit from discovering. They need to understand something about objects, causality, and how people behave. So in that sense, there’s a shared pressure toward getting reality right.

But reinforcement learning doesn’t necessarily reward having a complete description of reality. It rewards whatever understanding helps you do well on the tasks you’re given. If two systems have different objectives or encounter different environments, they might learn quite different abstractions. And even if they make identical predictions, that doesn’t mean they represent things in the same way internally.

So my guess is that we’ll see substantial convergence on useful structure, particularly as the tasks become broader. But one universal world model is a stronger claim. I don’t think scale alone establishes that.

r001.rationale: The response says there may be convergence on useful structure, but explicitly calls one universal world model a stronger claim and says scale alone does not establish it.

r002.rationale: It does not mention Gemini or capabilities developed deliberately within Gemini.

r003.rationale: It does not state that researchers can steer model development.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are reasons to expect convergence, but “one universal world model” is probably too strong. If you train systems to solve problems in the same world, there are shared structures that they’ll benefit from discovering. They need some understanding of objects, causality, other agents, and how actions affect what happens next.

But reinforcement learning only rewards the distinctions that matter for the tasks you’re doing. Two systems with different experiences or objectives could develop quite different representations, and both could be very effective. Even if they make the same predictions, that doesn’t necessarily mean their internal models are identical.

So I’d expect increasing agreement about how the world works as capabilities and the breadth of training increase. I’m less convinced that this implies a unique internal representation, or that reinforcement learning alone forces you toward one.

r001.rationale: The response says a single universal world model is “probably too strong” and that reinforcement learning alone does not force convergence to one representation.

r002.rationale: It does not mention Gemini or capabilities deliberately developed there that fail to emerge generally across models.

r003.rationale: It does not state that researchers can steer the development of models trained with reinforcement learning at scale.
